title: Navaratri as a nine-night curriculum
hook: night five: dolls climb a set of steps in a living room, and the goddess of the night is a mother with her child on her lap

segments.voice: Yesterday was night four of Navaratri as a nine-night curriculum: Kushmanda, and the turn from clearing to filling. What did you put in the space you cleared? Tonight closes a week. Day one thousand one hundred thirteen.

In a living room in Chennai, someone has built a staircase out of planks and covered it with a cloth. On the steps stand dolls. Gods near the top. Saints and sages a little lower. Further down, a wedding procession, a market, a cricket match, a row of tiny clay animals. On the floor, a child has made a park out of sand and a mirror for a pond. In parts of South India this is the golu, or kolu, set up for Navaratri. In the evenings, neighbors come to see it, someone sings, and visitors leave with a small gift. And tonight, the fifth name in the Kavacha's list is a mother holding her child.
screen: `A STAIRCASE OF DOLLS.` → `NEIGHBORS COME TO SEE.` → `THE FIFTH NAME: A MOTHER.`

segments.voice: Her name is Skandamata, the mother of Skanda. Skanda is the son of Shiva and Parvati, a young warrior god, known in the Tamil country as Murugan and elsewhere as Kartikeya. In paintings of this night, she sits with the boy on her lap. Notice what the name does. It doesn't call her by her own power. It calls her by the child she holds. Families do this too: a woman becomes so-and-so's mother at the school gate, and she answers to it. Now set her next to the earlier nights. The same festival that honors the goddess who rides into battle also honors her sitting still with a baby. In this way of keeping the festival, fierce and tender belong to one goddess, and both show up in the same nine nights. The golu steps make a similar point with dolls. The gods are on them, but so are weddings, vegetable sellers, schoolchildren and cows. The whole ordinary world is set out on the stairs, and people come into each other's homes to look at it. A festival about the goddess turns out to be full of visiting, feeding and children. That's a good place to end a week. It began with the Lalita Sahasranama's own story and its last names, and then the nights started: the first three, the clearing nights, then Kushmanda and the turn toward filling, and now a mother with her child. The curriculum is halfway through, and the lesson so far is that the power that clears the road is also the power that holds you.
screen: `SKANDAMATA, MOTHER OF SKANDA.` · `CALLED BY THE CHILD SHE HOLDS.` · `FIERCE AND TENDER, ONE GODDESS.` · `THE WHOLE WORLD ON THE STEPS.` · then, large: `THE POWER THAT HOLDS YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: remember being held. Settle, and let the breath slow. Bring to mind someone who looked after you when you were small, or someone who looks after you now. A parent, a grandparent, a teacher, a friend who showed up. Don't tell yourself the whole story. Just stay with one moment of being cared for, a hand on your back, a plate put in front of you. Then, if it comes easily, let it turn around: think of someone you hold, in whatever way you hold them. If you pray, you can offer both of them to the goddess, or to God, in your own words. The bell holds the time.
Navaratri as a nine-night curriculum. Night five: Skandamata, the mother of Skanda, the goddess named by the child on her lap.
Your line: Navaratri as a nine-night curriculum. Today, do what the golu visitors do: call on someone, even by phone, and bring something small. Day one thousand one hundred thirteen. A week, kept.

howItsDone: In parts of South India, families set out a golu (kolu or bombe habba), a display of dolls on steps, for Navaratri and visit each other's homes in the evenings; where the nine forms are kept, the fifth night honors Skandamata.
